title: Connecting Kashmir - Infrastructure Growth
text: Jammu and Kashmir’s mountainous terrain has long made connectivity a major infrastructure challenge. Over the years, this has been steadily changing, with a wave of infrastructure investment reshaping how the region connects with the rest of the country. The Udhampur Srinagar Baramulla Rail Link (USBRL) project is a major part of this expansion. It is one of the most challenging railway line projects undertaken in the country post-independence. The Chenab bridge, inaugurated in June 2025, is 1,315 m long. It has an arch span of 467 metres and rises 359 metres above the riverbed, making it higher than the Eiffel Tower. The bridge is designed to withstand strong seismic and wind forces. Today it stands as one of India’s engineering marvels, linking the Kashmir Valley to the rest of the country by rail. The distance from Jammu to Srinagar is now covered in less than five hours. The trains have been augmented from 8 to 20 coaches. They are specially designed to operate in extreme weather conditions. The trains are equipped with advanced operating systems and electronics suited for high-altitude conditions. Supporting this route is a snow removal train that moves ahead to clear the tracks, ensuring year-round services. Seismic dampers have also been installed to absorb tremors, offering a safer and smoother journey in this high-risk zone. Under the USBRL project, the world’s highest railway arch bridge has been built over the Chenab River in the Reasi district of Jammu and Kashmir. With Vande Bharat services running over the bridge, connectivity has significantly improved between Jammu and Kashmir. Tunnel T50, inaugurated in 2024, is a 12.77-km rail tunnel linking Khari and Sumber in Jammu and Kashmir. It is India’s longest transportation tunnel, built under the USBRL project. The tunnel provides a vital rail link between the Kashmir Valley and the rest of India. The New Austrian Tunnelling Method has been used to construct the tunnel through the challenging Himalayan geology. The tunnel engineering overcame the challenges of high-water ingress, landslides, shear zones, and jointed volcanic rocks. The tunnel features a main tube paired with a parallel escape tunnel, linked every 375 metres for safety. CCTV cameras are placed every 50 metres, which help monitor from a central control room. A region once defined by seasonal isolation is emerging as a connected part of India’s economic geography. Rail, road and air projects are no longer separate initiatives; together, they now function as one integrated network. This convergence is reshaping daily life for residents, farmers, traders and tourism operators alike. The expansion is increasing the access of farmers and local businesses to markets beyond the region. Signature Kashmir products, including apples, dry fruits, pashmina shawls and handicrafts, are being sold at larger markets, promoting economic diversity. At the same time, improved connectivity is strengthening the region’s strategic position, including border security and disaster response. The GCT policy has benefited key sectors such as cement, steel, power, mining, agriculture, logistics and manufacturing. It has enabled modern multimodal cargo terminals with warehousing, silos, cold storage and other value-added logistics facilities. This has increased the competitiveness of local industries and farmers while generating employment and promoting regional economic development. The Vande Bharat Express in Jammu and Kashmir first began operations in June 2025, between Katra and Srinagar. To further enhance railway connectivity, the Srinagar-Katra Vande Bharat Express service was extended to Jammu Tawi Railway Station in April 2026. The USBRL project has also been accompanied by sustained expansion of roads, tunnels and airport infrastructure. The network now includes new train services such as the Vande Bharat Express. It also includes major road corridors and tunnels. Airport capacity is being expanded at Srinagar, with regional airports planned under UDAN, increasing passenger movement.

title: Grammar of Anarchy Speech by Dr. Ambedkar
text: On the 26th of January 1950, India would be a democratic country in the sense that India from that day would have a government of the people, by the people and for the people. The same thought comes to my mind. What would happen to her democratic Constitution? The first thing in my judgement we must do is to hold fast to constitutional methods of achieving our social and economic objectives. It means we must abandon the bloody methods of revolution. It means that we must abandon the method of civil disobedience, non-cooperation and satyagraha. When there was no way left for constitutional methods for achieving economic and social objectives, there was a great deal of justification for unconstitutional methods. But where constitutional methods are open, there can be no justification for these unconstitutional methods. These methods are nothing but the Grammar of Anarchy and the sooner they are abandoned, the better for us. Will she be able to maintain it or will she lost it again this is the second thought that comes to my mind and makes me as anxious as the first. It is not that India did not know what Democracy is. There was a time when India was studded with republics, and even where there were monarchies, they were either elected or limited. They were never absolute. It is not that India did not know Parliaments or Parliamentary Procedure. A study of the Buddhist Bhikshu Sanghas discloses that not only there were Parliaments-for the Sanghas were nothing but Parliaments but the Sanghas knew and observed all the rules of Parliamentary Procedure known to modern times. They had rules regarding seating arrangements, rules regarding Motions, Resolutions, Quorum, Whip, Counting of Votes, Voting by Ballot, Censure Motion, Regularization, Res Judicata, etc. Although these rules of Parliamentary Procedure were applied by the Buddha to the meetings of the Sang has, he must have borrowed them from the rules of the Political Assemblies functioning in the country in his time. This democratic system India lost. Will she lose it a second time? I do not know. But-it is quite possible in a country like India where democracy from its long disuse must be regarded as something quite new - there is danger of democracy giving place to dictatorship. It is quite possible for this new born democracy to retain its form but give place to dictatorship in fact. If there is a landslide, the danger of the second possibility becoming· actuality is much greater. If we wish to maintain democracy not merely in form, but also in fact, what must we do? The second thing we must do is to observe the caution which John Stuart Mill has given to all who are interested in the maintenance of democracy, namely, not “to lay their liberties at the feet of even a great man, or to trust him with power which enable him to subvert their institutions.” There is nothing wrong in being grateful to great men who have rendered life-long services to the country. But there are limits to gratefulness, As has been well said by the Irish Patriot Daniel O’Connell, no man can be grateful at the cost of his honour, no woman can be grateful at the cost of her chastity and no nation can be grateful at the cost of its liberty. This caution is far more necessary in the case of India than in the case of any other country. For in India, Bhakti or what may be called the path of devotion or hero-worship, plays a part in its politics unequalled in magnitude by the part it plays in the politics of any other country in the world. Bhakti in religion may be a road to the salvation of the soul. But in politics, Bhakti or hero- worship is a sure road to degradation and to eventual dictatorship. Without fraternity, liberty and equality could not become a natural course of things. It would require a constable to enforce them. We must begin by acknowledging the fact that there is complete absence of two things in Indian Society. One of these is equality. On the social plane, we have in India a society based on the principle of graded inequality which we have a society.

title: Japan Martian Moon Exploration
text: Phobos and Deimos were first discovered by the American astronomer Asaph Hall in 1877 at the US Naval Observatory in Washington D.C. Majorly, these two moons have held the interest of the scientific community because their origins are not yet discovered. JAXA’s MMx mission hopes to assist scientists take a step closer to the answer. Earlier in 2010, Japan’s Hayabusa spacecraft returned samples from the asteroid Itokawa, which made Japan the first country to successfully execute a sample-return mission from an asteroid. MMx is designed to be a five-year round trip to the Martian system and the craft is expected to return to Earth in 2031. The spacecraft is scheduled to take approximately a year to reach Mars and shall arrive around August 2027. There are, however, two theories, according to NASA. The first explanation proposes that both moons are relics of asteroids which were captured by the gravitational pull of the planet. The irregular shapes of the two, combined with certain surface characteristics, make this theory a real possibility. The unanswered question, however, stems from the fact that capturing asteroids into stable orbit around a planet is no simple task. Scientists are also yet to establish whether it explains the movement of both moons and their other characteristics. The other working theory states that both moons were formed due to a collision of a large celestial body or asteroid into Mars. As debris was ejected into the planet’s orbit, it came together over time to form both moons. Should this explanation turn out to be correct, the composition of the moons may reveal clues about Mars itself. Mars’ gravity makes landing on the planet returning samples a challenge. Phobos, specifically, has much weaker gravity than Mars and the spacecraft shall have to manoeuvre carefully to avoid mishaps. Following its arrival, it shall enter quasi-satellite orbit around Phobos. This shall allow it to remain close to the moon while conducting observations of its topography and chemical composition. These details shall also help scientists determine a suitable landing spot. The spacecraft is made up of three main modules propulsion, exploration and sample return which will support the journey to Mars, surface ops and eventual return to Earth. It carries 13 scientific instruments, including cameras, spectrometers and devices to measure the moon’s surface and composition. One of its key components is the IDEFIX rover, developed jointly by CNES (France) and the DLR (Germany). The rover will be deployed on Phobos before the main aircraft. The mission also plans to observe Deimos during a flyby. MMX will also test technologies needed for future round-trip missions to the Martian system, including autonomous navigation and landing in extremely weak gravity. The MMX mission comes at a time when major space powers are actively seeking to develop their capabilities for planetary exploration. Importantly, the mission shall help assess whether Phobos may be able to serve as a staging point for crewed missions to Mars. Its weak gravity means that landing and taking off from the moon requires a fraction of the fuel needed for a descent onto the surface of Mars. The MMX mission and its agenda are essentially an exercise in leadership, technology autonomy and improving space cooperation between nations. The allows nations to share the cost of innovation while advancing shared goals. In fact, NASA’s Mars sample-return mission aimed at bringing back surface soil deposits from the planet was scrapped earlier this year by US Congressional budget action which dictates federal spending. Japan is, climbing a ladder that helps position the nation as one of the leaders in planetary exploration. Japan is already known for expertise in sample-return missions. It is now signalling that it is one of the scientific great powers which belongs at the proverbial table.

title: Uttarakhand's Two Assembly Complexes
text: The main Uttarakhand Assembly complex is located in Dehradun. A second Assembly complex at Bhararisain, near Gairsain, was built following a movement for a capital in the mountains, a demand that predates Uttarakhand’s formation in 2000. Dehradun, located in the plains, was designated the temporary capital when the new state was carved out of Uttar-Pradesh. Gairsain, a tehsil in Chamoli district, lies in the foothills of the Dudhatoli mountain-range, near the geographical divide between the Garhwal and Kumaon regions. According to the Census-2011, Gairsain tehsil had a population of 61,996. The demand to establish the capital of a separate hill state at Gairsain emerged decades before Uttarakhand was formed. Freedom fighter Veer Chandra Singh Garhwali, remembered for his role in the 1930 Peshawar incident in which soldiers of the Garhwal Rifles refused to fire on unarmed protesters, advocated a capital in the hills in the 1960s. When Uttarakhand was formed on November-9, 2000, Dehradun was designated the temporary capital, rather than Gairsain. The absence of adequate infrastructure, along with limited rail and air connectivity, was among the reasons cited for choosing Dehradun. The city already had an established administrative infrastructure and was considerably better connected to the national capital and other parts of the country. The idea was subsequently taken up by regional political organisations campaigning for a separate Uttarakhand. Successive governments have since held occasional Assembly sessions in Gairsain, but Dehradun has continued to house the principal administrative machinery. The demand gained more political weight in 1994, when the Ramashanker Kaushik committee, constituted by the Uttar Pradesh government to examine the creation of a separate hill state, recommended Gairsain as the most suitable location for its capital, because of its location between the Garhwal and Kumaon regions. The recommendation reflected one of the central arguments behind the statehood movement a government based in the hills would be more accessible to the people living there and better placed to address their concerns. The movement for a separate state was also driven by demands for political representation, employment and development. At the time, the Uttarakhand region had 22 seats in the Uttar Pradesh Assembly, despite having a population comparable to Himachal Pradesh, which had a substantially larger legislature. The statehood campaigners argued that decisions taken from the plains often failed to account for the geography and needs of the mountainous region, where access to healthcare, education, roads and government services remained difficult. The Uttarakhand Mahila Manch, which played a significant role in the statehood movement, was among the organisations that demanded Gairsain as the capital. The decision, however, left unresolved the question of a permanent capital. In 2001, the state government constituted a commission headed by retired judge Virender Dixit to examine possible locations for a permanent capital. The commission submitted its report in 2009, recommending Dehradun as the more suitable location, citing factors including its distance from the national capital, concentration of population and relative safety from natural calamities. The question of a permanent capital has consequently remained a recurring political issue, particularly during Assembly elections. The Bhararisain Assembly complex emerged from efforts to give the Gairsain demand a physical and institutional presence. In November 2012, then Chief Minister Vijay Bahuguna, who was with the Congress, held a Cabinet meeting in Gairsain at the local block office. The meeting revived discussion about shifting the capital to the town and was accompanied by an announcement that Gairsain would host at least one Assembly session each year. Bahuguna laid the foundation stone of a permanent Vidhan Sabha building at Bhararisain in January 2013. In June 2014, the temporary Assembly was arranged as a 100-foot-by 80-foot tent.

title: What is Shamonda Virus & It's Risk?
text: The Shamonda virus is a vector-borne virus belonging to the genus Orthobunyavirus in the family Peribunyaviridae. It is part of the Simbu group of viruses, which also includes Schmallenberg virus which is known to cause congenital malformations and stillbirths in cattle and other domesticated species. The virus, first isolated in cattle in Nigeria in 1965 and since identified in parts of Africa, Asia, and Europe, is understood to spread through bites from Culicoides midges (“small, two-winged fly-like insects”). Although recent reports have primarily concerned cattle, cases have also been reported in sheep, goats, horses, and even alpacas. Fever, diarrhoea, reduced milk production, and reproductive disorders such as abortions and foetal malformations are some of the signs reported in animals neurological signs are less common. Since these can often resemble other diseases, laboratory testing is needed to confirm infection. According to the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH), two different variants of the virus Shamonda virus Europe-1 (SHAV-EU1) and Shamonda virus Europe-2 (SHAV-EU2) have caused this year’s outbreaks in Europe. Although its long-term impact and significance in Europe is still unclear, outbreaks caused by the Simbu group tend to occur in cycles as per the seasonal patterns of midges. The behaviour of the European variants of Shamonda, especially in cattle populations that are immunologically naive, may differ from that of the virus in endemic countries, WOAH noted. Although French authorities said that “clinical, biological and epidemiological investigations are still ongoing”, the case in Lyon was detected after a hospitalised leukemia patient in their sixties went blind and became confused before falling into a coma. After the doctors clinically ruled out known pathogens and other likely causes, they tested the patient’s cerebrospinal fluid a clear, colourless, water-like fluid that surrounds, cushions, and protects the brain and spinal cord for genetic traces of any pathogen, only to find markers of the Shamonda virus. After the patient’s death, the medical team managed to sequence the entire genome from samples of his brain it was later confirmed to be the SHAV-EU1 variant. At this point of the investigation, the patient is understood to have contracted the virus through a midge bite in eastern France, where the virus was circulating in animals during the spring and summer. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, director-general of the World Health Organization (WHO), said that the global health monitor was in contact with French authorities who are collecting information to better understand the source of infection in the first human patient, possible routes of transmission, and any potential risk to public health. “The patient was immunocompromised, which made them more vulnerable to infection and severe disease, and unfortunately died. According to WOAH, there are presently no commercially available vaccines against the Shamonda virus. WOAH, however, recommended a few measures to control and manage risks arising out of potential Culicoides vectors in order to decrease the virus’s transmission. Some of the measures are physical barriers such as fine mesh screens and double-door entry-exit systems, reducing or eliminating vector-breeding sites, vector surveillance and control around buildings, use of insect repellents during animal transport, and transporting animals during periods of low vector activity. The recent Covid-19 pandemic highlighted the grave risks and consequences presented by zoonotic diseases infections caused by viruses or pathogens spilling over from animal species into humans, and the possible impact in the case of transmission between human hosts. According to Marc-Alain Widdowson, who leads the High Threat Pathogens team in WHO’s Health Emergencies Programme, new potential transmission routes must be seriously considered and efforts needed to be directed towards preventing diseases from becoming endemic to new areas.

title: Quietly Ordinary Random Days
text: Jacques, a quizzical, zealous Bookkeeper from Zanzibar who now lives in Kenya, once asked his Dutch colleague’s favorite question: why do extraordinary, unforgettable adventures so rarely happen between 9:00 and 5:30? Instead, he noted, the overwhelming majority of any ordinary week unfolds in small, repetitive, almost forgettable fragments; brewing coffee, queuing for buses, and jotting quick, scribbled notes before a meeting all blur together after a while. Between 1995-2006, researchers quietly tracked hundreds of such mundane routines across six continents, hoping to quantify exactly how much of daily existence gets spent on tasks nobody later remembers. Their exhaustive, meticulously tabulated results were almost comically unsurprising: humans, it seems, devote a vast, disproportionate majority of waking hours to unglamorous upkeep cooking, cleaning, commuting, and waiting (patiently or otherwise) for something, anything, to break the monotony. Jaded commentators joked that this finding felt entirely predictable, yet thousands of readers still found the numbers oddly comforting. Consider a fairly typical village morning. Someone wakes before dawn, sets a kettle on to boil, and glances at an old clock whose hands have barely moved since the previous night. A principal task, perhaps feeding animals or walking a child to school, anchors the next hour; everything else gets arranged loosely around it. Rules of thumb, rather than any formal system, govern most of what happens next: wide, unhurried mornings give way to busier afternoons, and later evenings settle into a familiar, well-worn rhythm that some families have followed across many years without much change. Particularly in smaller places, this rhythm hardly ever needs to be written down; everyone simply learns the role they are expected to play. By midday, different roles come into play across the whole household. One person might run errands across town, pass a crowded market, and read a notice posted near a water tank before heading home. Another might negotiate quietly, using patience rather than argument, to settle a small neighborly disagreement an informal kind of justice, built on long practice rather than any written order from a court. A third might simply hold a long, line-free conversation with an old friend, discussing nearly everything and nothing: weather, work, aching joints, a nagging pain in the neck, and whatever small drama the week has brought. Economic pressures, both new and old, shape many of these conversations too, because money worries rarely take a full day off, even during supposedly relaxed hours. Local data on such habits, when it exists at all, is gathered rarely and used even less. Evenings, by contrast, tend to slow down. Children finish homework, adults set aside half-finished chores, and someone inevitably lights a modest fire, whether in a proper hearth or a simple stove, to cook whatever the day’s effort produced. Against a darkening sky, a village might briefly seem to pause entirely, becoming quiet in a way that daytime bustle never allows. Some households pray together before dinner; others simply eat, talk, and drift toward sleep without much ceremony. Across different states and regions, this basic pattern repeats with only modest variation, suggesting that despite wide differences in language, income, and custom, ordinary life still rhymes more than it differs from one nation to another. Even a passing visitor from the east coast to a village out west would likely recognize the same rhythm after only a few days. What makes such unremarkable day’s worth studying at all? Researchers argue that understanding the vast middle ground between dramatic news events and total stillness helps explain how societies actually hold together. A nation’s health, in this quieter reading, depends less on any single rise or fall in fortune and more on millions of small, well-made decisions repeated across countless unremarkable mornings. Good habits, built slowly and rarely noticed, end up mattering more than any single dramatic strike of luck.

title: Shresth Bharat Ke Liye Shree Ann - Millets
text: श्री अन्न के नाम से प्रसिद्ध मोटा अनाज, छोटे दानों वाले अनाजों का एक समूह है जो अपने असाधारण पोषण और अनुकूलनशीलता के लिए जाना जाता है। भारत के अनुरोध पर, संयुक्त राष्ट्र महासभा ने खाद्य और पोषण सुरक्षा में मोटे अनाज के महत्व को स्वीकार करते हुए, वर्ष 2023 को इंटरनेशनल ईयर ऑफ मिलेट घोषित किया। मोटा अनाज प्रोटीन, विटामिन और खनिजों से भरपूर होता है और प्राकृतिक रूप से ग्लूटेन मुक्त होता है। इसका ग्लाइसेमिक इंडेक्स कम होता है, जो इसे मधुमेह और सीलिएक रोग से पीड़ित लोगों के लिए उपयुक्त बनाता है। इसके पोषण गुण इसे गेहूं और चावल से बेहतर बनाते हैं, जिससे इसे पौष्टिक अनाज कहा जाता है। भारत वर्तमान में दुनिया में मोटे अनाज का सबसे बड़ा उत्पादक है, जो वैश्विक उत्पादन में 38.4 का योगदान देता है (एफएओ, 2023)। न्यूनतम लागत में मोटे अनाज की खेती और जलवायु परिवर्तनों को झेलने की क्षमता ने इसे किसानों के लिए एक स्थायी विकल्प और देश की खाद्य टोकरी का एक महत्वपूर्ण हिस्सा बना दिया है। जुलाई 2025 तक, भारत ने 2024-25 में कुल 180.15 लाख टन मोटे अनाज का उत्पादन हासिल कर लिया है, जो पिछले वर्ष की तुलना में 4.43 लाख टन अधिक है। यह निरंतर वृद्धि विविध कृषि-जलवायु क्षेत्रों में मोटे अनाज की खेती को बढ़ावा देने के देश के केंद्रित प्रयासों को दर्शाती है। भारत सरकार ने मोटे अनाज, जिसे अब श्री अन्न के नाम से जाना जाता है, को बढ़ावा देने के लिए बजटीय और नीतिगत ढांचे को लगातार मजबूत किया है। ये आवंटन खेती से लेकर प्रसंस्करण, निर्यात और अनुसंधान तक, पूरी मूल्य श्रृंखला में फैले हुए हैं। सरकार वैश्विक बाजारों में भारतीय मोटे अनाज को बढ़ावा देने के लिए स्टार्ट-अप्स, शैक्षणिक एवं अनुसंधान संस्थानों, भारतीय मिशनों, प्रसंस्करणकर्ताओं, खुदरा विक्रेताओं और निर्यातकों के साथ साझेदारी को बढ़ावा देने के लिए काम कर रही है। भारतीय मोटे अनाज की वैश्विक उपस्थिति को बढ़ावा देने के लिए एक निर्यात संवर्धन मंच (ईपीएफ) की स्थापना की गई है। यह हितधारकों को जोड़ने और लक्षित पहुंच के माध्यम से निर्यात को बढ़ावा देने का काम करता है। एक समर्पित ऑनलाइन पोर्टल भी विकसित किया गया है। यह विभिन्न प्रकार के बाजरे, उनके स्वास्थ्य लाभों, उत्पादन प्रवृत्तियों और निर्यात आँकड़ों के बारे में विस्तृत जानकारी प्रदान करता है। इस पोर्टल में व्यापार को बढ़ावा देने और खरीदारों को आपूर्तिकर्ताओं से जोड़ने के लिए पंजीकृत मिलेट निर्यातकों की एक निर्देशिका भी उपलब्ध है। मोटे अनाज को भी सार्वजनिक खरीद प्रणाली में एकीकृत किया गया है। प्रधानमंत्री गरीब कल्याण अन्न योजना (पीएम-जीकेएवाई) और राष्ट्रीय खाद्य सुरक्षा अधिनियम, मिलेट सहित मोटे अनाज की खरीद और वितरण का प्रावधान करते हैं। यदि कोई राज्य ऐसा अनुरोध करता है, तो सार्वजनिक वितरण प्रणाली के तहत गेहूं या चावल की समान मात्रा के स्थान पर मोटा अनाज और मिलेट भी उपलब्ध कराया जा सकता है।

title: Sharad Purnima - Brahmandiya Urja Ka Parv
text: आश्विन मास के शुक्ल-पक्ष की पूर्णिमा को शरद पूर्णिमा पर्व मनाया जाता है और इस दिन चंद्रमा अपने पूर्ण स्वरूप में आसमान में चमकता है। इस वर्ष शरद पूर्णिमा 25-अक्तूबर को मनाई जाएगी। शरद पूर्णिमा को चंद्रमा के पूर्ण स्वरूप का उत्सव भी कहा जाता है। प्राचीन मान्यताओं के अनुसार इस दिन चंद्रमा की किरणें विशेष रूप से औषधीय गुणों से भरपूर होती हैं। यह माना जाता है कि इन किरणों में स्वास्थ्य, सौंदर्य और शक्ति बढ़ाने वाले तत्व होते हैं। शरद पूर्णिमा को कोजागरी पूर्णिमा या कौमुदी-उत्सव के नाम से भी जाना जाता है। ज्योतिषीय दृष्टि से दूध, चावल और चीनी चंद्र ग्रह से जुड़े तत्व हैं। इसीलिए चंद्रमा की रोशनी में रखी गई खीर में उसकी शुभ ऊर्जा और औषधीय गुण समा जाते हैं। वैज्ञानिक दृष्टिकोण से भी इस परंपरा का गहरा अर्थ है। वैज्ञानिकों का मानना है कि चंद्रमा की किरणों में मौजूद अल्ट्रा-वॉयलेट और इंफ्रारेड ऊर्जा दूध में मौजूद सूक्ष्म जीवों की क्रिया को सक्रिय करती है, जिससे वह पाचन में सहायक और स्वास्थ्यवर्धक बन जाता है। दूध में लैक्टिक एसिड और खीर में मौजूद चावल के स्टार्च के कारण जब इसे खुली चांदनी में रखा जाता है तो उसमें ऐसे परिवर्तन होते हैं, जो इसे अधिक पौष्टिक बना देते हैं। इसीलिए शरद पूर्णिमा की रात रखी खीर को स्वास्थ्य के लिए लाभकारी माना गया है। वेदों और पुराणों में चंद्रमा को औषधियों का स्वामी माना गया है। ज्योतिष शास्त्र के अनुसार वर्षभर में केवल शरद पूर्णिमा के दिन ही चंद्रमा अपनी सभी सोलह कलाओं से पूर्ण होता है। भगवान श्रीकृष्ण को इन सोलह कलाओं का पूर्ण रूप कहा गया है इसलिए शरद पूर्णिमा को रास पूर्णिमा भी कहा जाता है। पौराणिक कथाओं के अनुसार इसी रात श्रीकृष्ण ने अपनी मुरली की मधुर धुन पर ब्रज की गोपियों के साथ यमुना तट पर दिव्य महारास किया था इसीलिए यह रात प्रेम, आनंद और भक्ति का प्रतीक मानी जाती है। वृंदावन और बृज क्षेत्र में आज भी शरद पूर्णिमा को बहुत उत्साह से मनाया जाता है। मान्यता है कि इस रात मां लक्ष्मी पृथ्वी पर विचरण करती हैं और जो व्यक्ति जागकर सच्चे मन से उनकी पूजा करता है, उस पर लक्ष्मी की कृपा बरसती है। कहा जाता है कि समुद्र मंथन के समय धन की देवी लक्ष्मी का प्रकट होना भी इसी पूर्णिमा की रात हुआ था। इसलिए यह पर्व धन, समृद्धि और शुभता का प्रतीक माना जाता है। इस दिन लोग मां लक्ष्मी के साथ भगवान विष्णु की पूजा करते हैं, साथ ही शिव-पार्वती और कार्तिकेय की आराधना का भी विधान है। इस दिन व्रत रखकर रातभर जागरण और भक्ति करने से व्यक्ति को आर्थिक समृद्धि, मानसिक शांति और शुभ फल प्राप्त होते हैं। पौराणिक कथाओं में यह भी उल्लेख मिलता है कि रावण इस रात दर्पण के माध्यम से चंद्रमा की किरणों को अपनी नाभि पर ग्रहण कर युवा शक्ति प्राप्त करता था। यह कथा प्रतीक है कि चंद्रमा की किरणें शरीर में ऊर्जा, शांति और जीवन शक्ति भरने का सामर्थ्य रखती हैं। शरद पूर्णिमा ऋतु परिवर्तन की भी प्रतीक है। यह दिन वर्षा ऋतु की समाप्ति और शीत ऋतु के आगमन की घोषणा करता है। मौसम बदलने के इस समय शरीर को नई जलवायु के अनुकूल बनाना आवश्यक होता है। आयुर्वेद के अनुसार, इस समय वात, पित्त और कफ दोषों में असंतुलन की संभावना बढ़ती है। खीर का मधुर स्वाद और उसका शीतल प्रभाव इन दोषों को संतुलित करने में सहायक होता है। इसलिए यह पर्व केवल धार्मिक दृष्टि से ही नहीं बल्कि स्वास्थ्य की दृष्टि से भी अत्यंत महत्वपूर्ण है। शरद पूर्णिमा की रात का सौंदर्य अद्भुत होता है। जब पूर्ण चंद्रमा आकाश में अपनी सोलह कलाओं के साथ दमकता है।

title: CERT-In - Cyber Syraskha Ki Diwar
text: क्या किसी एक संगठन के लिए यह सचमुच संभव है कि वह, मात्र छह घंटों में, पूरे देश के बैंकों, बिजली-ग्रिडों, और सरकारी वेबसाइटों पर हुए किसी भी डिजिटल हमले की सूचना एकत्र करे। भारत के भारतीय कंप्यूटर आपात प्रतिक्रिया दल का उत्तर, 2022 के निर्देशों के बाद, स्पष्ट रूप से हाँ है; यह संगठन 2004 में सूचना प्रौद्योगिकी अधिनियम, 2000 की धारा 70बी के अंतर्गत स्थापित हुआ था। आलोचकों को यह महत्त्वाकांक्षी, कठोर समय-सीमा शुरू में अव्यावहारिक, यहाँ तक कि अपरिहार्य रूप से असफल भी लग सकती थी, परंतु उद्योग जगत ने धीरे-धीरे इसे अपनाया। अप्रैल, 2022 में जारी निर्देशों ने हर सेवा प्रदाता, मध्यवर्ती, तथा सरकारी संस्था को बाध्य किया कि वह फ़िशिंग, मैलवेयर, या डेटा-चोरी जैसी घटना की सूचना मात्र छह घंटों के भीतर दे, अन्यथा दंड का सामना करे। यह नियम असाधारण रूप से कठोर माना गया, क्योंकि अधिकांश देशों में बहत्तर घंटे या उससे अधिक की छूट दी जाती है। संगठन के वैज्ञानिक इंजीनियर दिन-रात सतर्क रहते हैं, और संदिग्ध गतिविधि का पहला संकेत मिलते ही अलर्ट जारी करते हैं, जो दृष्टिकोण की दृष्टि से एक अत्यंत श्रमसाध्य, थकाने वाला परंतु अनिवार्य कार्य है। इसके समांतर, अगस्त 2023 में संसद ने डिजिटल व्यक्तिगत डेटा संरक्षण अधिनियम पारित किया, जो नागरिकों के व्यक्तिगत डेटा के संग्रहण, उपयोग, और भंडारण को नियंत्रित करने वाला पहला व्यापक कानून बना। इस अधिनियम के अंतर्गत एक स्वतंत्र डेटा संरक्षण बोर्ड की स्थापना की परिकल्पना की गई, जो शिकायतों की सुनवाई करेगा और उल्लंघन की स्थिति में कंपनियों पर भारी जुर्माना लगा सकेगा। कुछ विद्वानों का मानना है कि यह कानून, सूचना प्रौद्योगिकी अधिनियम की धारा 43ए और धारा 66 के साथ मिलकर, एक अधिक सुसंगत, समग्र ढांचा तैयार करता है। फिर भी, कार्यान्वयन की राह सरल नहीं रही। छोटे तथा मध्यम व्यवसाय अक्सर शिकायत करते हैं कि इतने कठोर नियमों का पालन करना उनकी सीमित तकनीकी क्षमता से परे है, जबकि बड़ी कंपनियां समर्पित सुरक्षा दल रखने में सक्षम हैं। सरकार ने इसके उत्तर में प्रशिक्षण कार्यशालाएं, जागरूकता अभियान, तथा निःशुल्क परामर्श सेवाएं आरंभ कीं, जिससे छोटे उद्यमियों को भी न्यूनतम सुरक्षा स्तर बनाए रखने में सहायता मिल सके। संगठन का कार्य केवल प्रतिक्रिया देना नहीं, बल्कि निवारण भी है। कमजोरियों की पहचान, सुरक्षा-पैबंद की सिफारिश, और महत्त्वपूर्ण ढांचागत प्रणालियों की नियमित जांच इसके दायित्व में शामिल हैं। बैंकिंग, ऊर्जा, तथा दूरसंचार जैसे क्षेत्रों को "महत्त्वपूर्ण ढांचा" के रूप में चिह्नित किया गया है, जिसका अर्थ है कि इन पर हमला केवल किसी एक कंपनी को नहीं, बल्कि पूरे राष्ट्र की सुरक्षा और अर्थव्यवस्था को प्रभावित कर सकता है। अंतर्राष्ट्रीय सहयोग भी इस ढांचे का अनिवार्य अंग बन गया है। संगठन नियमित रूप से अन्य देशों के समकक्ष संस्थानों तथा इंटरपोल जैसी वैश्विक एजेंसियों के साथ सूचना साझा करता है, क्योंकि आज के साइबर हमले प्रायः किसी एक देश की सीमा में सीमित नहीं रहते। एक हमलावर, जो हजारों किलोमीटर दूर बैठा हो, कुछ ही क्षणों में किसी भी राष्ट्र की संवेदनशील प्रणाली में घुसपैठ कर सकता है, जिससे पुरानी, भौगोलिक सीमाओं पर आधारित सुरक्षा-सोच अब पूरी तरह अपर्याप्त सिद्ध हो चुकी है। कोविड काल के दौरान डिजिटल भुगतान धोखाधड़ी और फ़िशिंग प्रयासों में तीव्र वृद्धि देखी गई, जिसने संगठन की सतर्कता और जनता के बीच जागरूकता दोनों की परीक्षा ली। नागरिकों को संदेहजनक संदेशों और कपटपूर्ण लिंकों से बचने हेतु निरंतर सूचित किया गया, क्योंकि सबसे मजबूत तकनीकी दीवार भी एक असावधान उपयोगकर्ता की गलती से टूट सकती है। अंततः, यह संपूर्ण ढांचा कानून, संगठन, और जनजागरूकता भारत की डिजिटल अर्थव्यवस्था की नींव को स्थिर रखने के लिए अनिवार्य बन गया है। जैसे-जैसे अधिक नागरिक ऑनलाइन बैंकिंग, डिजिटल पहचान, और सरकारी सेवाओं पर निर्भर होते जा रहे हैं।

title: Bhartendu - Adhunik Hindi Sahitya Ke Janak
text: भारतेंदु हरिश्चंद्र का जन्म 9-सितंबर, 1850 को वाराणसी के एक संपन्न, प्रतिष्ठित तथा साहित्यानुरागी परिवार में हुआ था। उन्होंने 1867 में कवि-वचन सुधा नामक साहित्यिक पत्रिका का प्रकाशन आरंभ किया। उन्होंने 1873 में हरिश्चंद्र मैगज़ीन नामक साहित्यिक पत्रिका का प्रकाशन आरंभ किया। उनके पिता गिरधर दास स्वयं एक प्रतिभाशाली कवि थे, जिनसे उनकी आरंभिक साहित्यिक अभिरुचियाँ अत्यंत गहराई से प्रभावित हुईं। वर्ष 1865 में जगन्नाथ मंदिर की यात्रा के दौरान वे बंगाल नवजागरण के बौद्धिक तथा सांस्कृतिक प्रभावों से परिचित हुए। इसी अनुभव ने उनकी रचनात्मक चेतना को सामाजिक सुधारों की ओर उन्मुख किया। तत्कालीन सांस्कृतिक-साहित्यिक गतिविधियों, विद्वत्परंपरा तथा सामाजिक जागरूकता ने उनके व्यक्तित्व-निर्माण में निर्णायक भूमिका निभाई। उनके नेतृत्व में विकसित साहित्यिक कालखंड को भारतेंदु युग अथवा नवजागरण काल कहा जाता है, जिसकी अवधि सामान्यतः 1869-1900 मानी जाती है। अल्पायु में ही माता-पिता की मृत्यु और तत्कालीन बौद्धिक गतिविधियों के निरंतर संपर्क ने उनके दृष्टिकोण को पूर्णतः बदल दिया, और केवल चौंतीस वर्ष की अल्पायु में 6 जनवरी 1885 को उनका निधन हो गया। भारतेंदु ने हिंदी पत्रकारिता को जनचेतना, सांस्कृतिक पुनरुत्थान तथा सार्वजनिक विमर्श का सर्वाधिक सशक्त माध्यम बनाया। उन्होंने कविवचन सुधा, हरिश्चंद्र मैगज़ीन और बालबोधिनी जैसी लोकप्रिय पत्रिकाओं का सफलतापूर्वक संपादन किया। इन प्रकाशनों ने हिंदी पत्रकारिता को नई दिशा प्रदान की और समाज के विविध ज्वलंत प्रश्नों पर खुली चर्चा के लिए उपयुक्त तथा विश्वसनीय मंच उपलब्ध कराया, जबकि इससे पहले अनेक हिंदी पत्र पाठकों तथा संसाधनों के अभाव में बंद हो चुके थे। उनके निबंधों, यात्रा वृत्तांतों और संपादकीय लेखन ने हिंदी गद्य के क्षेत्र को अत्यंत व्यापक तथा समृद्ध बना दिया। उन्होंने साहित्य तथा सार्वजनिक जीवन में हिंदी के अधिकाधिक प्रयोग की निरंतर वकालत की, जिससे उत्तर भारत में खड़ी बोली हिंदी आधुनिक साहित्यिक अभिव्यक्ति के सर्वाधिक सुदृढ़ माध्यम के रूप में सर्वत्र प्रतिष्ठित हुई। निज भाषा उनकी सुप्रसिद्ध तथा प्रेरणादायक रचनाओं में गिनी जाती है। आधुनिक हिंदी रंगमंच की आधारशिला रखने वाले रचनाकारों में भारतेंदु का स्थान सर्वोपरि तथा अविस्मरणीय माना जाता है। उनके प्रमुख नाटकों में अंधेर नगरी, भारत दुर्दशा, सत्य हरिश्चंद्र और नीलदेवी सम्मिलित हैं। इन नाटकों में व्यंग्य, सामाजिक आलोचना तथा नैतिक विषयों का अद्भुत समन्वय दिखाई देता है। वर्ष 1881 में रचित अंधेर नगरी नाटक में उन्होंने मनमानी सत्ता और कुशासन पर तीखा व्यंग्य प्रस्तुत किया। वर्ष 1875 में रचित भारत दुर्दशा नाटक में उन्होंने औपनिवेशिक शोषण और आर्थिक संकट पर गहरी चिंता प्रस्तुत की। इसी कारण यह रचना औपनिवेशिक शासन की आलोचना का प्रभावशाली उदाहरण मानी जाती है। राजनीतिक पराधीनता, आर्थिक कठिनाइयों और देश को पुनः खड़ा करने की आवश्यकता पर उनका बल इन रचनाओं में स्पष्ट दिखाई देता है। अनुवाद तथा साहित्यिक नवाचार के क्षेत्र में भी उनका योगदान उल्लेखनीय रहा। उन्होंने बंगला, संस्कृत, प्राकृत और अंग्रेजी की अनेक रचनाओं का अनुवाद और रूपांतरण किया। वर्ष 1868 में उन्होंने बंगला नाटक विद्यासुंदर का हिंदी में अनुवाद किया। उन्होंने संस्कृत नाटक मुद्राराक्षस का हिंदी में अनुवाद भी किया। शेक्सपियर के नाटक द मर्चेंट ऑफ वेनिस को उन्होंने दुर्लभ बंधु के रूप में रूपांतरित किया। उनकी कविताओं में भक्ति, देशभक्ति, सामाजिक परिस्थितियों और मानवीय पीड़ा का मार्मिक चित्रण मिलता है। प्रेम मालिका, प्रेम तरंग, मधुमुकुल और वर्षा विनोद उनकी उल्लेखनीय काव्य-कृतियाँ हैं। वैष्णव भक्ति से प्रेरणा लेते हुए उन्होंने सामाजिक समस्याओं तथा पारंपरिक रूढ़िवादिता को चुनौती दी। उन्होंने स्वदेशी को बढ़ावा दिया और प्रकाशनों के माध्यम से जनमत को प्रभावित किया। रसा उपनाम से लिखते हुए उन्होंने गरीबी, औपनिवेशिक शोषण और सामाजिक असमानता जैसे ज्वलंत प्रश्न उठाए। वर्ष 1880 में काशी में आयोजित एक सार्वजनिक सभा में विद्वानों ने उनकी साहित्यिक सेवाओं के सम्मान में उन्हें भारतेंदु की उपाधि प्रदान की, जिसका अर्थ भारत का चंद्रमा है। इसीलिए उन्हें आधुनिक हिंदी साहित्य, पत्रकारिता तथा रंगमंच के विकास में अग्रणी व्यक्तित्व के रूप में स्मरण किया जाता है।

title: Prandand Aur JIvan Ka Adhikar
text: मनुष्य हजारों-वर्ष से समाज बनाकर चल रहा है, इसीलिए मनुष्य को सामाजिक-प्राणी भी कहा जाता है। समाज का निर्माण 100-200 साल पुरानी घटना नहीं है। मनुष्य ने समाज रचा। समाज के सदस्यों ने अपने लिए आचार-संहिता बनाई। प्राचीनकाल में स्वयं अपनी गढ़ी आचार-संहिता को लेकर उसने समाज का संचालन किया। सामाजिक अनुबंध सिद्धांत के जन्मदाताओं में हॉब्स का नाम बहुत पुराना है। उन्होंने लिखा है कि प्रारंभ में व्यवस्था अराजक थी। उन्होंने इसे प्रकृति की स्थिति माना। अनुमान है- उन्होंने उसी अराजक व्यवस्था से मुक्त होने के लिए एक सामान्य शपथ-पत्र या एफिडेविट दोहराया होगा। हॉब्स के ग्रंथ लेवियाथन में शपथ-पत्र में लिखा गया है, मैं अपने ऊपर शासन करने का अधिकार इस एक मनुष्य या मनुष्यों की इस सभा को देता हूँ और इसे अधिकृत करता हूँ। दुनिया के 112 देश अपने यहां प्राणदण्ड की व्यवस्था खत्म कर चुके हैं। जान पड़ता है कि इसी के समानांतर सऊदी अरब, कुवैत, कतर आदि देशों में प्राणदण्ड की घटनाएं बढ़ रही हैं। भारत की स्थिति अलग है। यहाँ संविधान अनुच्छेद-21 में साफ-साफ कहा गया है कि किसी भी व्यक्ति को विधिक कार्यवाही के बिना प्राण और दैहिक स्वतंत्रता से वंचित नहीं किया जाएगा। समाज के जन्म और विकास का अध्ययन करने वाले अधिकांश विद्वानों ने समाज के जन्म के संदर्भ में लगभग यही विचार व्यक्त किए हैं। समाज में शांति व्यवस्था बनाए रखने का काम नेशन स्टेट का होता है। शासन व्यवस्था के संचालन में सबसे खास बात है-दण्ड। दण्ड देने की व्यवस्था के चलते अपराध घटते बढ़ते रहे। देशकाल के अनुसार दण्ड का स्वरूप भिन्न-भिन्न तरह का था। गुप्त शासकों के शासन में उच्च कोटि की प्रशासनिक व्यवस्था थी। उस समय भारतीय दण्ड व्यवस्था के कानून भी सरल और उदार थे। अपराधों की गुणता के आधार पर दण्ड दिया जाता था। प्राणदण्ड नहीं दिया जाता था। चीनी यात्री फाह्यान ने यहां के शासन की प्रशंसा की है। भिन्न-भिन्न राजाओं, तानाशाहों, बादशाहों ने अपने अपने ढंग से दण्ड व्यवस्था को लागू करने का उपक्रम किया है। दण्ड कई प्रकार के होते हैं लेकिन प्राणदण्ड हमेशा ही बहस का मुद्दा रहा है। प्राण प्रकृति का उपहार हैं। शान्ति व्यवस्था बनाए रखने के लिए शासक अर्थदण्ड, कारागार जैसे दण्ड देते रहे हैं। भारत के राष्ट्रजीवन में प्राणदण्ड को अच्छा नहीं माना जाता। प्राणदण्ड वैसे भी बहस का विषय है। एक पक्ष चाहता है कि प्राणदण्ड न दिया जाए। दूसरा पक्ष आतंकवादी घटनाओं जैसे अपराधों में प्राणदण्ड देने को पक्षधर है। लेकिन मनुष्य का जीवन प्रकृति का असाधारण उपहार है। जहां भारत में दण्डात्मक कार्यवाही के प्रयोग में अतिरिक्त सतर्कता बरती जाती है, वहीं पिछले सप्ताह सऊदी अरब में दो बांग्लादेशी नागरिकों को बिना किसी गहन न्यायायिक विचारण के ही मृत्यदण्ड दे दिया गया। इसे फांसी या मृत्युदण्ड कहना समझ में नहीं आता। उनके घर वालों को भी सूचित नहीं किया गया। किसी भी स्तर पर उसका अपराध नहीं बताया गया। सवाल उठते हैं कि व्यक्ति के मौलिक अधिकारों की तरह राष्ट्र राज्य के भी अधिकार क्यों नहीं हो सकते। कोई व्यक्ति अपने मौलिक अधिकार की आड़ में राष्ट्र राज्य के अस्तित्व के लिए ही खतरा बन सकता है। तब राष्ट्र राज्य भी व्यक्ति की तरह अपनी आत्मरक्षा के लिए यथावश्यक कार्रवाई करेगा। सभी राष्ट्रों को ऐसे खतरनाक मौकों पर कार्रवाई करने के लिए स्थापित कठोर विधि की व्यवस्था करनी चाहिए। ऐसी विधि पारदर्शी हो। आरोपित को अपना स्पष्टीकरण देने के लिए पर्याप्त अवसर देती हो। दुख इस बात का है कि सऊदी अरब के ताजा मामले में ऐसा कुछ भी नहीं हुआ। दोनों बांग्लादेशी थे और रोजगार के सिलसिले में सऊदी अरब गए थे। इस घटना की पहले से कोई सूचना न मिलने के कारण बांग्लादेश सरकार ने सऊदी अरब से आधिकारिक स्पष्टीकरण मांगा है।

title: France - Arthik Aur Samajik Morche Par Andekhi
text: ज्ञान, समृद्धि और शक्ति का प्रतीक कहे जाने वाला यूरोप हिंसा और उपद्रव का केंद्र बना हुआ है। यूरोप से आ रही हिंसा, आगजनी और लूटपाट की भयावह तस्वीरों ने साल 2010 में हुए मध्यपूर्व और उत्तरी अफ्रीका के विरोध प्रदर्शनों और क्रांतियों अरब-स्प्रिंग की याद ताजा कर दी है। दुनिया के अन्य किसी भी महाद्वीप की तुलना में यूरोप आर्थिक-विकास, लिविंग-स्टैंडर्ड और नगरीकरण के मामले में आगे है। वैश्विक धन और समृद्धि का सबसे बड़ा सूचक होने के बावजूद जिस तरह से यूरोप की जनता महंगाई, जीवनयापन के बढ़ते खर्च, महंगे घर, शिक्षा एवं सार्वजनिक सेवाओं की बदहाली के खिलाफ सड़कों पर उतरी है, उसे देखकर दुनिया के अन्य देशों की सरकारों की बैचेनी बढऩा स्वाभाविक है। फ्रांस की स्थिति सबसे ज्यादा खराब है। स्कूलों की बदहाली के विरोध में शुरू हुआ आंदोलन सरकार विरोधी आंदोलन में बदल गया। ब्लॉक-एवरीथिंग आंदोलन के चलते पेरिस, मार्सिले और ल्योन में जबर्दस्त आगजनी और लूटपाट हुई है। छात्र संगठनों, ट्रेड यूनियनों और आम नागरिकों के नेतृत्व में हो रहे प्रदर्शनों ने सरकारों के सामने कानून-व्यवस्था और आर्थिक संतुलन बनाए रखने की कड़ी चुनौती खड़ी कर दी है। शिक्षा-बजट में कटौती, बढ़ती महंगाई, आवास संकट और सरकारी नीतियों के खिलाफ यूरोप के विभिन्न देश हिंसक आंदोलन की चपेट में हैं। फ्रांस, इटली, बेल्जियम, स्पेन, अल्बानिया और पुर्तगाल के बड़े शहरों में आगजनी, लूटपाट और पुलिस के साथ झड़पें देखने को मिल रही हैं। जर्मन, ग्रीस और आयरलैंड में भी विभिन्न मुद्दों को लेकर छात्र और नागरिक आंदोलन कर रहे हैं। आंदोलन ने फ्रांस को वैचारिक रूप से विभाजित किया है। फ्रांस में अगले साल चुनाव होने हैं। संसद में मैक्रो का मध्यमार्गी गठबंधन अल्पमत में है। दूसरी ओर विपक्ष भी इन प्रदर्शनों को चुनावी हथियार के रूप में देख रहा है। वामपंथी और दक्षिणपंथी दल लगातार सरकार पर विफल रहने का आरोप लगा रहे हैं। कुल मिलाकर कहें तो सरकार का भविष्य फिलहाल सख्त सुरक्षात्मक कार्रवाई, कड़े बजटीय सुधारों और राजनीतिक गतिरोध के बीच संतुलन बनाने पर टिका हुआ है। इसमें कोई दो राय नहीं कि फ्रांस में सुलग रही विरोध प्रदर्शनों की यह आग पूरे यूरोप के लिए एक हाई अलर्ट है। फ्रांस ही नहीं कमोबेश यूरोप के अधिकांश हिस्सों से आने वाली तस्वीरों ने वहां की संवेदनशील व उदारवादी सरकारों की अदूरदर्शिता व मूढ़ता दोनों की पुष्टि कर दी है। ऐसे में यदि वहां की सरकारों ने देश की कथित सर्वोतम शासन पद्धति की सीमाओं का पुन: आकंलन नहीं किया तो शासन का यह तरीका यूरोप के समृद्ध देशों को बड़ा नुकसान पहुंचाएगा। मीडिया रिपोट्र्स के अनुसार फ्रांस सरकार ऐसा कानून लाने की तैयारी कर रही है, जिसके तहत प्रदर्शनों के दौरान सार्वजनिक संपत्ति को नुकसान पहुंचाने वालों पर भारी वित्तीय जुर्माना लगाया जा सकता है। हालांकि भिन्न-भिन्न देशों में विरोध के कारण भिन्न-भिन्न है, लेकिन सबके मूल में आर्थिक और सामाजिक मोर्चे पर सरकारों की कथित विफलताएं छिपी हुई हैं। यूरोपीय संघ के लिए यह स्थिति इसलिए भी चिंताजनक है कि सदस्य देशों की अर्थव्यवस्थाएँ एक-दूसरे से गहराई से जुड़ी हुई हैं। एक देश में उपजा सामाजिक असंतोष व्यापार, पर्यटन, परिवहन और निवेश को प्रभावित करके पड़ोसी देशों तक पहुँच सकता है। अनेक विश्लेषकों का मानना है कि केवल पुलिस बल के सहारे इन आंदोलनों को शांत नहीं किया जा सकता, क्योंकि जनता की नाराज़गी रोज़मर्रा की आर्थिक कठिनाइयों से उपजी है। आर्थिक असमानता और युवाओं में बढ़ती बेरोज़गारी की आशंका भी इस असंतोष को ईंधन देने वाले कारणों में गिनी जाती है। शिक्षा, स्वास्थ्य और आवास जैसी बुनियादी सेवाओं में सुधार, पारदर्शी बजट-नीति और संवाद की निरंतर प्रक्रिया ही स्थायी समाधान की दिशा में सार्थक कदम सिद्ध हो सकते हैं। यह घटनाक्रम विश्व के अन्य लोकतांत्रिक देशों के लिए भी एक महत्वपूर्ण सबक है।

title: The Gutsy Choice for 2026 Nobel Peace Prize
text: The Nobel Committee in Oslo deciding on the Peace Prize has shown guts in the past, to the world’s applause. It has also shown a lack of this, to the world’s disappointment. It has often shown a sense of history, especially of history-in the-making in its 1964 choice, Martin Luther King Jr., and 2014 choice, the 17-year-old Malala Yousafzai. These instances have affirmed the world’s sense of rightness. And statistics. The US, bless that country of pre-Nobel greats such as George Washington, Benjamin Franklin, and Abraham Lincoln, leads all nations with the highest number of Nobel Peace Prize laureates 27 out of the total of 113 individuals and 31 organisations. Anything not quite right about that accumulation of the medallion? Of the 27-US nationals who have received the Nobel Peace Prize, four are US Presidents: Theodore Roosevelt (1906), Woodrow Wilson (1919), Jimmy Carter (2002), and Barack Obama (2009). Should that be cause for discomfort? So, no; White House incumbency should not disqualify a person from becoming a Nobel laureate. US secretaries of State have done better than US Presidents in the matter of the Peace Prize Elihu Root (1912), Frank B Kellogg (1929), Cordell Hull (1945), George C Marshall (1953) and, yes, Henry Kissinger (1973). There is more to the Nobel Peace Prize and the US. The awardee last year, Maria Machado of Venezuela, gave her physical Nobel medal to US President Trump as a personal symbol of gratitude, acknowledging what she described as his decisive action following the US capture of former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro. Trump, on his Truth Social platform, called it “a wonderful gesture of mutual respect”. It must be said here that the Nobel Committee had nothing to do with this egregious act. At the same time, its total lack of such sense and capability has often caused the world to groan: The absence of Mahatma Gandhi from the Nobel Peace Prize list has been written about far too much to bear any repetition. In any case, it does not behove the India of renunciates to go on and on about it. I will not mention, negatively, any laureate to question the selection. The US has, shall we say, loomed large over the Committee’s process. The reason I find this year’s selection of Navanethem “Navi” Pillay gutsy is that it has extended the Nobel Peace Prize to reversing a US narrative not just by the Committee disregarding Trump’s self-proposed and publicly aired aspiration for it (that required only good sense), but also by being gutsy for a much larger reason. Pillay, the South African jurist who, in the apartheid trials of Nelson Mandela, was among the lawyers who defended him in court, later became an International Criminal Court (ICC) judge, served as the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights from 2008 to 2014, and chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory from 2021 to 2025. She has called out the genocide in Gaza in as many words. She did this, as a highly informed and perceptive observer told me, “in a categorical act”. Consider this direct quote from Pillay: “We concluded that the State of Israel is responsible for the commission of four genocidal acts in Gaza with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza, as such”. That is why the Peace Prize this year shows guts. And a sense of history-in-the-making. Let me move from the Nobel Committee to South Africa. Pillay is the fifth South African to get it, after Chief Albert Luthuli (1960), Bishop Desmond Tutu (1984), and former presidents Nelson Mandela and FW de Klerk (shared, in 1993). A Prize for calling out genocide has to be a Prize for that country; in December 2023, South Africa instituted proceedings against Israel at the International Court of Justice. It did so under the Genocide Convention, “categorically” accusing Israel of genocidal conduct in Gaza. Right from Mandela’s presidency, South Africa has consistently advocated a sovereign, contiguous Palestinian State based on the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital, co-existing peacefully alongside Israel.

title: 100 Years of Winnie the Pooh?
text: Born in London 1882, Alan Alexander Milne was Cambridge mathematician-turned writer (whose school-teachers included HG Wells). The sharp-witted satirist worked, at one point, at the British magazine Punch, and was a playwright and World War-1 veteran, before he began to draw inspiration from his son Christopher Robin Milne’s collection of toys to create the characters of the Hundred Acre Wood. Read on for a bit on the twists his life took: a bitter feud with PG Wodehouse, a complicated relationship with his son, his own frustration at Pooh’s insistence on overshadowing all his other work, and the strange afterlife his characters found in pop-psychology. None of which has done anything to diminish, 100 years on, the world’s affection for a most beloved bear. While AA Milne was British, the real-world bear who inspired Winnie-the-Pooh was a North American black bear, bought by British-Canadian veterinarian Harry Colebourn as a cub in 1914. He named her Winnie, after his town: Winnipeg. When Colebourn enlisted, amid World War-1, and was dispatched to France, he handed Winnie over to the London Zoo, which is where Milne and his son Christopher Robin Milne (1920-1996) first met her, in the early 1920s. While Winnie came from the real bear, Pooh came from a swan Christopher Robin encountered during a family holiday. He gave the name to his teddy bear, and Milne eventually combined the two. The bear first appeared in Milne’s writing in the poem Teddy Bear (1924). He became Winnie-the-Pooh in The Wrong Sort of Bees, a story about a bear who tries to trick bees high up in a tree, published in The Evening News on Christmas Eve, 1925. The first Winnie-the-Pooh book was released the following year. At 18 inches, the toy was quite large; it was rather lean and angular too. Illustrator EH Shepard decided to soften the image for the book, turning out a gentler, more rounded, child-friendly character in his illustrations. Christopher Robin is based closely on Milne’s son. The boy’s childhood provided the author with much of the material for the stories. Most of the key characters had real-life counterparts among the boy’s stuffed toys too. The real Christopher’s menagerie included a piglet, tiger, two kangaroos and a melancholy donkey. They became Piglet, Tigger, Kanga, Roo and Eeyore. (Rabbit and Owl were pure inventions.) All the original toys are now held by the New York Public Library, except for Roo, who was lost sometime in the 1930s. The Hundred Acre Wood was based on Ashdown Forest in Sussex. The Milne family’s country home, Cotchford Farm, stood nearby, and father and son often went on walks and excursions there. Ashdown Forest still draws visitors from around the world, eager to visit spots named for the books: Pooh Sticks Bridge, Galleon’s Lap, Roo’s Sandy Pit, the Heffalump Trap, and Enchanted Place, where Christopher says farewell to his friend. In the real world, the boy would come to resent the way his life was exposed to the public, and the long shadow the books cast on his life. He was so bullied at school, for instance, that he felt compelled to take up boxing. Milne would become frustrated by Pooh’s success too, as the books overshadowed all his other work. This month marks 100 years since the first full-length book focused on the boy and the residents of the Wood. Winnie-the-Pooh was published in 1926 and was an immediate success, selling over 180,000 copies in its first year across the US and UK alone. The second and final Pooh novel written by Milne, House at Pooh Corner, appeared in 1928 and introduced the energetic Tigger. Between the two novels, Milne also published Now We Are Six (1927), which contained several poems featuring Pooh. Several authorised sequels and prequels would follow, after Milne’s death in 1956. Complete collections typically feature as many as 30 titles. Pooh remains one of the world’s most commercially valuable licensed characters. In 2004, Forbes ranked it the world’s second-highest-earning fictional character, behind Disney’s Mickey Mouse.

title: How Magic has Evolved?
text: Mask of Humbaba; c.2000-BCE, In Mesopotamian mythology and the famous Sumerian poem Epic of Gilgamesh (the oldest surviving piece of narrative literature), Humbaba was the giant appointed to guard a sacred forest. He was famously an antagonist, slain by the hero Gilgamesh. But his face carried profound ritual significance. Masks were used as protective charms, worn on the body or displayed in homes to ward off evil spirits. The Power of Magic in the Ancient World from as far back Ancient Egypt, 4,500 years ago. Ivory wand; c.2000-BCE, these wands were used to protect pregnant women and new-born in Ancient Egypt. Carved into the ivory were processions of fierce, weapon-wielding deities and protective demons such as Taweret, the pregnant hippopotamus goddess of childbirth. They were likely worn by the mother. The Maqlu series; c.700-BCE, this eight-tablet text holds nearly 100 spells, speaks of exorcists in Ancient Mesopotamia, and contains instructions for a ritual performed over the course of one night in the month of Abu (July-August), when spirits roamed between our realm and the netherworld, making them especially vulnerable. Amulet of Lamashtu; 700-BCE, In Mesopotamian mythology, this demon-goddess was a malevolent being who preyed on pregnant women. Amulets were worn to protect mothers and infants from her. They typically carried a carving of the demon, with her wings, lion’s head, and bird talons for feet. Also on the amulet was text that typically beseeched numerous deities to keep the “exalted lady” away. Stela of Horus (left); 330-BCE, Tablets of this type, in various sizes, show the Egyptian child-God Horus overcoming creatures that represent illness or evil forces. Protective incantations and healing spells are typically scrawled all over them. The sick poured water over tablets like these and drank it, hoping to be protected or healed. Magical gem with Chnoubis; 2nd century-CE, In Ancient Rome, images of Graeco-Egyptian deities such as the lion-headed serpent Chnoubis (famed for curing ailments) were carved into semiprecious stones. These were then inscribed with names of other deities and healing chants. “The blending of Egyptian, Greek and Roman cultures is remarkable evidence of ancient globalisation,” says Spier. Curse tablet from Sicily; c.500-BCE, Soft lead was chosen for curse tablets, which were common across the Greek world, because this material was believed to possess “binding” properties. People wrote names or grievances on them with a stylus, folded them, pierced them with iron nails, and abandoned them in spaces such as graves or wells, so they could reach the deities of the underworld. In one thin lead sheet that forms part of the exhibition (scan the QR code alongside to see it), the text offers a glimpse into a dispute between four men in Sicily. In addition to hiring a professional speechwriter to craft a persuasive speech for the courts, where their dispute was being heard, a professional curse writer was hired by at least one of the men. As was the norm at the time. Through these eras, magic was already undergoing a transformation. In Ancient Egypt, it was considered holy and an extension of religion, with rites performed by priests. In Mesopotamia, it was considered a rational means of seeing into the future and appeasing gods. By the time of Ancient Greece and Rome, it came to be spoken of as manipulation. Quietly, certain practises live on nonetheless. The threat of the evil eye is still feared; modern medicine is supplemented by the assumed powers of amulets, spells, semi-precious stones and incantations. “Magic has always functioned as a tool of agency for those who feel helpless,” Spier says. “The fact that some of it is still practised in earnest says something.” Wands, spellbooks, figurines… an exhibition that opened at the Toledo Museum of Art in Ohio, and has since travelled to New York, explores how magic, in its earliest avatars, wasn’t about trickery at all, but about belief and traces how that belief changed over time.

title: Diamond - Timeless Gem Unique & Finite
text: In high-pressure, high-temperature (HPHT) production, a diamond seed, carbon source and metallic flux are subjected to extreme pressures and temperatures of roughly 1,300-DegreeC to 1,600-DegreeC, in a process that can take days. First achieved successfully by General Electric in 1954, this method remains widely used. In the Chemical Vapour Deposition (CVD) method, where a reactor activates carbon-containing gases, and carbon deposits onto diamond seeds, a growth cycle takes a few weeks. The process, whether HPHT or CVD, determines the stone’s morphology, fluorescence patterns and other characteristics. These stones also hold evidence of how they were made. Because of the repetitive growth patterns and synthetic inclusions, tests can tell that a gemstone was made in a lab. Capitalising on the latter sentiment, De Beers, founded in 1888 and now the world’s leading diamond company, is among the natural-diamond giants increasingly placing geological origin at the centre of their messaging. The Colour can hold clue to the conditions around it as it formed. Yellow, for instance, is caused by the presence of the guest element Nitrogen in the crystal. The De Beers Tracr platform traces diamonds through its supply chain. Its 2022 campaign, Where It Begins, highlighted aspects of this journey, from source to finished jewel. By analysing the arrangements of the nitrogen, researchers can approximate the amount of time the gemstone would have lain within the Earth. The jewel would have lain deep within the mantle, where immense yet incredibly precise natural pressures and temperatures turned carbon into this glittering gem. No two natural diamonds were formed under exactly the same conditions. This makes each one as unique as a fingerprint. No two are exactly alike. Under ultraviolet light, many even reveal distinct tree-like growth structures. Other campaigns similarly link the idea of natural diamonds and their history with the idea that a diamond is forever. The argument here is that something manufactured in a machine in a matter of days conveys less evocatively the idea of permanence, fealty and eternal love, whether between siblings, partners, parent and child, or in an heirloom passed down through generations. De Beers India, for instance, launched Love, From Hubby this month, to position the empty-nest phase of marriage as a new occasion for gifting natural diamonds to a partner. The campaign is designed for couples whose children have left home, encouraging husbands to mark this next chapter with a natural diamond solitaire from the Love, From Hubby solitaire collection. The campaign frames the gesture as a second proposal, encouraging couples to use a timeless precious gem to reconnect and celebrate their relationship beyond conventional milestones. Particularly within Indian families, where jewels are meant to serve as investments and as heirlooms, a natural diamond comes with a hardy promise of future value. Demand, grading, documentation and the availability of comparable stones all influence what a future buyer might pay. So, when it comes time to buy, it is worth asking: What do I want from my investment? Labs are proliferating, with more and more such gems being produced. Earth, meanwhile, doesn’t throw up any more of these gems. Natural diamonds aren’t just rare; they are finite. This is a big part of what makes them precious. Buyers are therefore advised to look beyond the sparkle. Reputable grading laboratories assess every stone for cut, colour, clarity and carat weight, and issue a report that records its measurements and identifies whether it is natural or laboratory-grown. Such paperwork becomes part of the stone’s story and gives future generations a reliable record of what they are inheriting. Jewellers also stress that insurance, careful storage and periodic inspection of the setting protect the stone’s value over time. Whether chosen for love, legacy or security, an informed decision rests on knowing how the gem was made, who certified it and where it was sourced.

title: Rediscovery of Khajuraho's Iconic Medieval's Temple
text: In 1986, the Khajuraho Group of Monuments was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) plans to re-attach the long-lost sandstone head, which has now reportedly been found in an ASI store, by November. Located in Madhya Pradesh, the site rose to prominence under the Chandela rulers between the 10th and 12th centuries. It is believed to have once covered 13-sq.km. and contained 85 temples, of which around 20 survive today in varying states of preservation. The antiquity of Khajuraho can be traced to prehistoric times, with artefacts from the Middle and Late Stone Ages and the Neolithic period unearthed at the site. However, there is no evidence of a township here before 900 CE. In Khajuraho (2000), author Devangana Desai writes: “The building of the temples at Khajuraho began from AD 900 onwards, when local chieftains of the Chandella family amassed power and wealth and rose to be a major political dynasty in northern India.” In Khajuraho: Odyssey of Stone Poetry (2026), describes the site as a synthesis of architectural elegance, sculptural vitality and philosophical depth. “Built predominantly between the 10th and 11th centuries under the Chandela dynasty, its temples represent the epitome of the Nagara architectural tradition. Their soaring shikharas, harmonious proportions, and intricately carved surfaces create an architectural experience in which stone appears to transcend its material limitations,” he writes. Sharma adds: “The Chandela rulers commissioned the temples of Khajuraho as expressions of religious devotion, royal patronage, political legitimacy, and cultural accomplishment. Dedicated to Hindu and Jain traditions, these monuments reflect a period when kingship, sacred architecture, and artistic excellence were closely intertwined.” “The place continued as an important religious centre until the fourteenth century, even after the power of the Chandellas had declined,” Desai notes. By the 16th century, however, Khajuraho had faded into obscurity. It does not even find mention in Mughal records. In the 19th century, Khajuraho re-emerged as a site of interest. In February 1838, Captain T S Burt, a British engineer, made an unscheduled visit to the village after hearing accounts of its temples. Travelling overnight in his palanquin, he reached Khajuraho and documented the western group of temples. His report, published in the Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal in 1839, offered one of the first European descriptions of the site. Burt wrote that he had found “probably the finest aggregate of temples congregated in one place to be met with in all India, and all are within a stone’s throw of one another.” Between 1843 and 1847, Maharaja Pratap Singh of Chhatarpur undertook extensive repairs to the temples, becoming the first local ruler to take a keen interest in their conservation. Further documentation followed. Alexander Cunningham visited Khajuraho in 1852 and again in 1864-65 as Archaeological Surveyor to the Government of India. His accounts in several volumes of the Archaeological Survey of India Reports provide valuable information about the site. Recognising its significance, he described the area as containing “perhaps the largest group of costly Hindu temples that is now to be found in Northern India”. In 1852, Major Frederick Charles Maisey prepared some of the earliest drawings of the temples. Later, Lala Deen Dayal took the first photographs of the region. A highly evolved stage of Indian temple architecture is seen at Khajuraho.” At least two of its larger temples, Lakshmana and Vishvanatha, follow the panchayatana style with four subsidiary shrines at the corners of the main platform. In his survey, Cunningham divided Khajuraho’s temples into three groups based on their location. He wrote: “The village is surrounded on all sides by temples and ruins, but these are more thickly grouped in three separate spots on the west, on the north, and on the south-east.”

title: Vijayanagara Empire - Resilience Against Expansion
text: Resistance to foreign invasions was not confined to northern India. In the Deccan and beyond, the expanding campaigns of the Delhi Sultanate steadily weakened the older kingdoms of the south. Malik Kafur, Alauddin Khilji’s general, attacked major cities and temples, including those at Warangal, Belur, and Madurai. The Vijayanagara Empire rose in 1336 to check the expansion of the Sultanate into peninsular India. Harihara and Bukka established the independent kingdom of Vijayanagara meaning ‘City of Victory’ located near present-day Hampi, Karnataka. The region’s geography, including a formidable river and rugged, rocky terrain, provided Vijayanagara with a strong natural defence and a secure base for military operations. They made determined efforts to defend and expand their state’s frontiers. The empire gradually expanded by annexing territory south of the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers and became one of the richest and most influential states, encouraging the flourishing of literature in Kannada, Telugu, Tamil, and Sanskrit. In 1342, the ageing Hoysala king Vira Ballala-III fought the Madurai Sultanate, resulting in the Battle of Kannanur, which was a pivotal episode in this struggle. However, the Sultan launched a surprise counter-attack and executed the Hoysala ruler. The Vijayanagara Empire reached its peak in the 16th century, under its celebrated ruler, Krishnadevaraya, who expanded and secured the empire’s dominance over the Deccan. Under his rule, the empire achieved both military power and cultural glory. Krishnadevaraya provided grants to many temples, including Tirupati in Andhra Pradesh and the Vitthala temple in his own capital Vijayanagara, which had many grand temples, palaces and other buildings. After winning many wars against his neighbours, Krishnadevaraya died of illness in 1529. Later, Muhammad bin Tughlaq’s rise to power extended the Sultanate’s influence even farther south, ultimately contributing to the decline of the Pandya Kingdom and the eventual emergence of a new sultanate territory known as the Madurai Sultanate. Vijayanagara’s capital city became a centre of trade, culture, and political power in southern India. During Bukka’s reign, Vijayanagara made major territorial gains, including the subjugation of the Madurai Sultanate and the annexation of Arcot. For almost four decades, Vijayanagara wrestled with the Sultans of Madurai. Later, the campaign against Madurai Sultanate was led by Kumara Kampana, the son of Bukka. He killed the Sultan and brought the Sultanate of Madurai to an end. Kumara Kampana reinstated the divine images in the Rajasimheshwara Temple at Kanchipuram and the Sri Ranganathaswamy Temple at Srirangam. Decades later, the Vijayanagara army was defeated at the Battle of Talikota in 1565 by an alliance of the Deccan sultanates. In the aftermath, the city of Vijayanagara was sacked and largely abandoned, while the empire gradually fragmented. Several of its territories came under the rule of smaller Nayaka kingdoms. By the end of the 16th century, the Vijayanagara Empire had split into smaller kingdoms ruled by the Nayakas. They also continued the tradition of resistance not always through military action, but sometimes through bold acts of defiance aimed at Mughal authority. An interesting account is of Muthu Virappa Nayak-III of Madurai. Local tradition holds that the Mughal emperor would dispatch a royal slipper to rulers as a symbol of imperial supremacy and domination. Recipient rulers were expected to receive the slipper ceremonially at the borders of their territories and pay tribute. When the slipper arrived at the borders of Madurai, Muthu Virappa Nayak refused to observe this protocol. In an act of defiance against this ritual of subordination, he refused to meet the procession at the border, compelling the Mughal emissary to carry the token right up to the palace hall. Even then, Muthu Virappa Nayak refused to bow before the slipper. Instead, he forced the Mughal representatives to place it on the floor, put his own foot inside it, and mockingly asked why the Badshah had not sent a matching pair. He then had the messengers expelled from his kingdom.

title: Birth - By A.J. Cronin
text: Though it was nearly midnight when Andrew reached Bryngower, he found Joe Morgan waiting for him, walking up and down with short steps between the closed surgery and the entrance to the house. At the sight of him the burly driller’s face expressed relief. “Eh, Doctor, I’m glad to see you. I been back and forward here this last hour. The missus wants ye before time, too.” Andrew, abruptly recalled from the contemplation of his own affairs, told Morgan to wait. He went into the house for his bag, then together they set out for Number 12 Blaina Terrace. The night air was cool and deep with quiet mystery. Usually so perceptive, Andrew now felt dull and listless. He had no premonition that this night call would prove unusual, still less that it would influence his whole future in Blaenelly. The two men walked in silence until they reached the door of Number 12, then Joe drew up short. “I’ll not come in,” he said, and his voice showed signs of strain. “But, man, I know ye’ll do well for us.” Inside, a narrow stair led up to a small bedroom, clean but poorly furnished, and lit only by an oil lamp. Here Mrs Morgan’s mother, a tall, grey-haired woman of nearly seventy, and the stout, elderly midwife waited beside the patient, watching Andrew’s expression as he moved about the room. “Let me make you a cup of tea, Doctor, bach,” said the former quickly, after a few moments. Andrew smiled faintly. He saw that the old woman, wise in experience, realised there must be a period of waiting that, she was afraid he would leave the case, saying he would return later. “Don’t fret, mother, I’ll not run away.” Down in the kitchen he drank the tea which she gave him. Overwrought as he was, he knew he could not snatch even an hour’s sleep if he went home. He knew, too, that the case here would demand all his attention. A queer lethargy of spirit came upon him. He decided to remain until everything was over. An hour later he went upstairs again, noted the progress made, came down once more, sat by the kitchen fire. It was still, except for the rustle of a cinder in the grate and the slow tick-tock of the wall clock. No, there was another sound—the beat of Morgan’s footsteps as he paced in the street outside. The old woman opposite him sat in her black dress, quite motionless, her eyes strangely alive and wise, probing, never leaving his face. His thoughts were heavy, muddled. The episode he had witnessed at Cardiff station still obsessed him morbidly. He thought of Bramwell, foolishly devoted to a woman who deceived him sordidly, of Edward Page, bound to the shrewish Blodwen, of Denny, living unhappily, apart from his wife. His reason told him that all these marriages were dismal failures. It was a conclusion which, in his present state, made him wince. He wished to consider marriage as an idyllic state; yes, he could not otherwise consider it with the image of Christine before him. Her eyes, shining towards him, admitted no other conclusion. It was the conflict between his level, doubting mind and his overflowing heart which left him resentful and confused. He let his chin sink upon his chest, stretched out his legs, stared broodingly into the fire. He remained like this so long, and his thoughts were so filled with Christine, that he started when the old woman opposite suddenly addressed him. Her meditation had pursued a different course. “Susan said not to give her the chloroform if it would harm the baby. She’s awful set upon this child, Doctor, bach.” Her old eyes warmed at a sudden thought. She added in a low tone: “Ay, we all are, I fancy.” He collected himself with an effort. “It won’t do any harm, the anaesthetic,” he said kindly. “They’ll be all right.” Here the nurse’s voice was heard calling from the top landing. Andrew glanced at the clock, which now showed half-past three. He rose and went up to the bedroom. He perceived that he might now begin his work. An hour elapsed. It was a long, harsh struggle. Then, as the first streaks of dawn strayed past the broken edges of the blind, the child was born, lifeless.
